articles.full_text:
Last updated: 11:15 08 Oct 2026 EDT, First published: 10:15 08 Oct 2026 EDT
Eastport Critical Metals CEO Daniel Major joined Steve Darling from Proactive to discuss the company’s diversified critical minerals portfolio in Botswana, recent rare earth drilling results and plans to advance its uranium, copper and nickel projects through 2026 and into 2027.
Major highlighted Botswana’s established mining industry, infrastructure and government support for mineral development. Eastport Critical Metals has six projects covering five commodities, with its portfolio focused on minerals that could benefit from growing global electrification and demand for critical raw materials.
A major focus is the company’s large-scale uranium project in northern Botswana, where an exploration target covering almost 300 square kilometres has been identified. Gravity surveys and additional geophysical work are underway to refine targets ahead of a drilling programme expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027.
The company is also advancing its rare earth project near Gaborone, where recent drilling returned an intersection exceeding 330 metres at 0.21% rare earths. Major said further assay results are pending as Eastport evaluates the scale and continuity of the mineralization and determines the next phase of exploration.
At its nickel-copper project near the Selebi mine, soil sampling has identified correlations between nickel-copper anomalies and the underlying geology. Eastport plans to conduct additional electromagnetic surveys to help define potential drilling targets.
Major said the company is continuing to evaluate opportunities across its broader portfolio while prioritizing its larger-scale projects. Depending on the development requirements of individual assets, potential strategies could include joint ventures, asset sales or spinning projects into separate companies.
Looking ahead, Major pointed to growing interest in rare earths and copper from both companies and governments, while also highlighting the potential for renewed investor attention toward uranium as global demand for critical minerals continues to grow.
Eastport’s diversified approach is designed to give the company exposure to multiple critical mineral markets while allowing it to advance projects according to their individual exploration and development potential.

The energy transition offers a window of opportunity to design in circularity from the outset
Decarbonisation and electrification are superseding the fuel-intensive economy, but they depend on the continuous availability of electricity networks, renewable energyrenewable energyEnergy derived from resources that are not depleted on timescales relevant to the economy, i.e. not geological timescales. generation, batteries, storage systems, and EVs that will only continue to rise in demand — along with the critical minerals inside them.
The minerals inside clean energy technology can either become tomorrow’s supply or tomorrow’s expense
As the first generation of clean energy technologies approaches the end of life, the system built around them will influence what happens to the critical minerals they contain. If the system is designed around one-way material flows, every new generation of EVs, batteries, and energy infrastructure will continue relying on virgin extraction. Rather than allowing the high-value materials already in circulation to become waste, a circular economy keeps them circulating at their highest value, securing future supply while closing the supply–demand gap.
Batteries mark our first step in redesigning the energy transition
Batteries constitute a major critical mineral value chain where circular strategies can be implemented at scale. When designed for circularity, batteries can deliver mobility services first, energy storage services next, and a secondary supply of critical minerals later.
The global deployment of EV batteries, each containing roughly 200kg of critical minerals, means that large stocks of cobalt, copper, graphite, lithium, nickel, and more are already present inside the economy. At the same time, the business models, regulations, repairrepairOperation by which a faulty or broken product or component is returned back to a usable state to fulfil its intended use. and resale networks, reverse logisticsreverse logisticsSupply chains dedicated to the reverse flow of products and materials for the purpose of maintenance, repair, reuse, refurbishment, remanufacture, recycling, or regenerating natural systems., second-life markets, and recycling systems that govern those batteries are still being configured. Our report, Leading the charge, sets out how this emerging value chain can be designed around circular economycircular economyA systems solution framework that tackles global challenges like climate change, biodiversity loss, waste, and pollution. It is based on three principles, driven by design: eliminate waste and pollution, circulate products and materials (at their highest value), and regenerate nature. principles from the outset. It identifies five high-leverage opportunities for collaboration across the value chain and marks the beginning of a multi-year programme to accelerate circularity across battery systems.
Building on that foundation, we are working with automotive manufacturers, battery designers and producers, recyclers, policymakers, and our wider Network to support collaboration across battery value chains and develop the evidence and enabling conditions to scale circular economy solutions. Through this, we aim to establish the circular economy as central to securing the energy transition as a whole — by keeping critical minerals in use, reducing exposure to volatile mineral markets, and sustaining rapid global electrification while reducing the need for primary extraction.

Do you want to help build the circular critical minerals system of the future? Help shape the debate and the market? We are looking for industry leaders, investors, policymakers, and innovators to join our sector-specific working groups and implementation projects.
Support our Critical Minerals mission
As a not-for-profit organisation, the Ellen MacArthur Foundation relies on philanthropic support to to deliver its mission. Our 2026 Small Cap Pick of the Year Iondrive (ASX: ION) has just detailed its plan to fund its first commercial rare earth recycling module in the USA.
ION’s “Deep Eutectic Solvent” tech is capable of recovering critical minerals from scrap/e-waste, things like batteries/black mass, printed circuit boards, permanent magnets and solar panels.
ION is currently applying that tech to recover rare earths from e-waste - planning to build a facility in the US set to be in Oklahoma, called “Oklahoma Module 1”).
Once built - each module (according to economics released by ION) is capable of producing US$243M post-tax NPV on just US$11.9M of development capital.
These numbers are per module, so it is easily scalable from a construction and financing standpoint, should the E-waste supply feed be secured.
We made ION our 2026 Small Cap Pick of the Year off the back of those numbers, see why here.
Today ION detailed its plan to secure US$18M in debt funding to be put toward getting that first module fully built - including all of the commissioning/ramp-up costs.
ION confirmed in today’s announcement that the funding is aiming to be a mix of:
- Senior Debt
- Government incentives
- US supply chain partners
Up to 80% (US$14.4M) could be guaranteed under a USDA program, here is that part of the proposed funding announced today:
(source)
ION also included in today’s announcement that it’s assessing a prepared industrial site in Latimer County, Oklahoma, that would come with existing infrastructure and transport access.
So ION also needs funding to set up the facility including site works, working capital and to get into production, which is why the debt (with more funding avenues hinted at) from today is more than the cost of a single module.
A ready-made site (mentioned today) could reduce the cost, time and complexity versus a greenfields build, which would also help support the financing and permitting process too.
We have written about why we think Oklahoma is the right place to be for ION - see that here: ION: announces US$15M in support to build heavy rare earth recycling module in Oklahoma, USA. G7 summit says rare earths urgent.
Spoiler - it's because ION would be placing itself right near a logical customer for its product - $7BN USA Rare Earth who have publicly said “third party feedstock” would be used in the ramp up stages of its magnet plants.
Especially for heavy rare earths which are almost impossible to find in the US. (source)
The 10 reasons why we made ION our 2026 Small Cap Pick of the Year
- ION doing magnet rare earths recycling in the USA - where there is the most urgency, money and attention.
China’s export restrictions on rare earths kick started the whole “US Critical Minerals” macro thematic.
Rare earths are receiving the most US government attention, the most capital from inside the US with the most urgency.
Which is why we think ION’s tech is being focused on the right critical mineral in the right jurisdiction at the right time.
- ION is moving fast - and the pieces are in place.
ION, for its rare earth business in the US already has:
- A binding agreement with America's largest e-waste processor (Colt Recycling) to supply feedstock
- Independent lab tests showing ION's tech recovers rare earths - including heavy rare earths (93.5% dysprosium, 96.5% neodymium, 96.5% praseodymium)
- A letter of support for up to ~US$15M from the Oklahoma Department of Commerce for a recycling plant
- A first production run underway for 1.4 tonnes of rare earth oxide due within 150 days
- Trump executive orders are positive for ION
The 20-July order forces US military contractors to prove "serious efforts" to source critical minerals domestically before they can import them - with a 1 January 2027 deadline on Chinese-origin materials in US defence systems.
(They either show they have tried or risk losing defence contracts)
Then there is the 30-July Presidential Determination that gives the Department of Commerce the power to ban exports of e-waste, black mass and magnets so they get recycled at home.
Two executive orders that will mean more capital going into potential domestic supply sources (like ION) and also more feedstock for a business like ION.
- The G7 group of countries is also bullish critical minerals recycling
In June the G7 group of nations (basically all the western big dogs) met and made explicit commitments to “boost recycling of critical minerals”. (source)
Specifically calling out urgency around China dominated rare earths supply - rare earths being critical inputs in advanced technologies like AI, robotics and advanced weaponry.
One stated G7 aim was to make recycling capacity account for a “significant share” of annual consumption by 2030. (source)
Remember ION’s binding agreement in the US is with a company inside the Elemental Holding Group which has operations across 20+ countries across four continents.
- Recycling can be a lot faster than mining
S&P Global's July 2026 study puts the average time from discovery to production at 16 years - and nearly 30 years for mines not yet operating, with permitting the main culprit. ION's modules bolt onto e-waste facilities that already exist, with US$11.9M of development capital per module - and its first rare earth oxide is due within 150 days. (S&P Global, Jul-2026)
- US$243M NPV for each module - ION can build multiples of them around the US (and more globally)
One of ION’s 2,400tpa rare earths “modules” has the following economics:
- ~US$243M post-tax NPV,
- US$62M EBITDA
- US$122M revenue, and
- US$11.9M of development capital
That company (Colt Recycling) ION has a binding agreement with, runs FOUR US e-waste facilities.
AND is part of the Elemental Holding Group which has 50+ licensed scrap/e-waste collection and processing hubs across three continents. (source)
So those modular plants can be plugged into a global network pretty quickly (IF they work) - at US$243M NPV each…
- A facility in Oklahoma, USA would be next door to $6BN USA Rare Earths which is explicitly looking for third party feedstock.
Oklahoma is where the US government just handed out a US$1.6BN funding deal to USA Rare Earth - which includes ~US$50M to expand a magnet manufacturing plant. (source)
USA Rare Earths has in the past explicitly mentioned “third party feedstock” would be used in the ramp up stages of its magnet plants.
Especially for heavy rare earths which are almost impossible to find in the US. (source)
Remember: ION can recover heavy rare earths from e-waste.
- Critical minerals recycling and processing tech is getting funded - by governments AND private capital, right now.
We are seeing a lot of capital flow into recycling tech companies - especially in the US for companies able to recover critical minerals.
We have already seen the US government back:
- Jan 2025: the Pentagon put US$5.1M into a recycler pulling rare earths from old electronics. (source)
- June 2026: the Department Of Energy put US$134M for heavy rare earth recovery from e-waste and scrap. (source)
- The Department Of War made a US$25M strategic investment in ReElement, and handed Energy Fuels a ~US$725M conditional loan for rare earths processing
And private capital get behind the following two deals this year alone:
- Noveon Magnetics (recycled magnets) raise US$215M (Jan 26).
- Cyclic Materials (rare earth recycling) raise US$75M (Jan 26)
We think ION is in a position with its US rare earths business to attract this sort of funding.
- ION’s tech works on other critical minerals too
ION has already shown it can recover:
- Silver from solar panels (85%+ recoveries at bench scale).
- Battery metals from scrap batteries (black mass) - 89% lithium, 100% nickel, 98.6% cobalt, 98.4% manganese with a pilot plant due for commissioning in Q4-2026, AND
- Copper, gold and silver from circuit boards.
ION’s underlying Deep Eutectic Solvent tech has also been shown to recover other critical minerals like gallium, antimony and indium (plus many more).
We think that once ION commercialises its tech in one domain, it can expand into other critical minerals.
- ION also has the “minerals processing” X factor
ION is also using its tech to solve extraction issues that miners have (getting a certain mineral out of a certain type of rock).
ION is currently focused on two markets for mineral processing:
- Cobalt (also a critical mineral where the US is import dependent) - ION signed a binding term sheet with Latitude 66 to apply its technology on concentrates that would be produced from Latitude's project in the EU (Finland). (Source)
- Nickel - ION is testing its tech on US sourced feedstock in the nickel industry. (Source)
Processing tech, when it works can be very valuable - like the company ION’s director Hugo Schumann was CFO of (Jetti Resources) which raised US$100M at a US$2.5BN valuation.
What we want to see next from ION
Produce and qualify rare earth oxide in the US
We want to see ION complete its first production run and get its rare earth product qualified with potential downstream customers.
Milestones

🔄 1.4 tonnes of mixed rare earth oxide produced.

🔲 First offtake or supply agreement
Non-dilutive funding OR downstream partnership for US rare earths facility
We want to see ION receive non-dilutive funding OR sign a commercialisation deal with a downstream partner.
Milestones

🔲 Strategic or downstream investment

Final Investment Decision on US rare earth plant

articles.title: OPEC+ Leaves November Oil Output Targets Unchanged Despite Gulf Supply Disruptions - Arise News
articles.summary: OPEC+ Leaves November Oil Output Targets Unchanged Despite Gulf Supply Disruptions  Arise News
articles.full_text:
The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and its allies, OPEC+, have agreed to keep their oil production targets unchanged for November, as continuing disruptions linked to the Iran war keep actual output significantly below members’ official quotas.
The decision was taken at the weekend at a virtual meeting of seven key members of the wider OPEC+ alliance, including: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman.
Nigeria was not part of the meeting because it has historically struggled to meet its OPEC production quota. Consequently, its priority has largely been to restore production capacity and meet its allocated quota rather than participate in the additional voluntary cuts undertaken by the seven countries.
In a statement issued after the meeting, the seven countries said they had agreed to maintain their September 2026 required production levels for November.
The producers also reiterated their commitment to achieving “full conformity” with the Declaration of Cooperation, which underpins the group’s efforts to coordinate crude oil production and manage market conditions.
The decision was broadly in line with market expectations, with the producers signalling that they are not yet prepared to make further adjustments to their output policy.
The development comes against the backdrop of continued disruption to oil exports from the Gulf region following the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Although flows through the Strait of Hormuz have improved, exports from several Gulf producers have continued to operate substantially below normal levels, leaving actual production below the targets set by OPEC+.
The gap between official production targets and actual output has become particularly significant this year. OPEC+ has been increasing its production targets after years of supply cuts, but much of the planned increase has not translated into physical barrels because of disruptions associated with the Middle East conflict.
OPEC data showed that the seven core producers pumped about 25 million barrels per day in August, an increase of roughly 630,000 barrels per day from July. However, that remained about 5 million barrels per day below their combined production levels before the Iran war in February.
The continuing supply constraints have provided support for crude prices even as the market has reacted to efforts by major economies to cushion consumers against higher energy costs.
Brent crude remained above $100 a barrel, having risen sharply from around $73 a barrel before the Iran war began in late February. The oil market’s tightness has also complicated OPEC+’s plans for determining production allocations for 2027.
The alliance has been conducting a review of members’ sustainable production capacity, a process considered crucial to determining how future production increases should be distributed among participating countries.
However, the review has been delayed as the conflict has made it more difficult to establish the production capacity that individual members will be able to sustain.
OPEC+ still has about 2 million barrels per day of production cuts covering most of its members, according to industry sources cited by Reuters. The outcome of the capacity assessment is expected to guide decisions on how any future increases will be allocated.
With the review delayed and uncertainty surrounding future production potential, significant changes to individual production quotas are unlikely before 2027.
The seven producers are due to meet again on November 1 to review market conditions and the outlook.
A separate OPEC+ body, the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee, also met on Sunday to assess developments in the global oil market. The committee, however, does not have the authority to determine production policy.
The combination of elevated prices, constrained physical supply and uncertainty over the duration of the Middle East conflict is therefore likely to keep the global oil market sensitive to geopolitical developments in the months ahead.

articles.title: Power Metallic Advances Nisk Project as Robotics Drives Critical Minerals Demand - Streetwise Reports
articles.summary: Power Metallic Advances Nisk Project as Robotics Drives Critical Minerals Demand  Streetwise Reports
articles.full_text:
Key Investor Takeaways
- Power Metallic's October 5, 2026, appointment of BBA as lead engineering consultant for the Nisk PEA positions the company for a first-half 2027 economic study based on the recent Lion resource.
- Eric Sprott's robotics article underscores long-term demand growth for critical minerals in automation and physical AI, providing thematic context for polymetallic explorers like Power Metallic.
- Lion's high-grade copper-PGE resource and recent deep extensions highlight expansion potential in a jurisdiction with critical minerals incentives.
- Environmental baseline studies and community engagement are advancing in parallel with the PEA, funded from existing cash.
- Power Metallic's metals basket (copper, nickel, palladium, platinum) aligns with electrification and technology supply chains that support broader robotics and automation trends, though it focuses on different elements than rare earth magnets.
- Five rigs are active, and a CA$28.2 million June 2026 financing provides a runway for ongoing drilling and studies.
- Peer positioning in critical minerals benefits from the same macro tailwinds Sprott identifies for rare earths in robotics applications.
A PEA Informs Scale and Direction
Power Metallic Mines Inc. (PNPN:TSXV; PNPNF:OTCQB; IVV1:FSE) is advancing its high-grade polymetallic Nisk project in Quebec just as mega investor Eric Sprott highlighted surging rare earth demand from the robotics sector. On October 5, 2026, the company reported it had appointed BBA Inc. to lead a Preliminary Economic Assessment (PEA) of the Lion and Nisk Main deposits, targeting completion in the first half of 2027. The study is expected to assess mining and processing options, infrastructure requirements, capital and operating costs, and preliminary project economics.
This PEA marks a transition for Power Metallic from resource definition toward evaluating a potential development case. The study will focus primarily on the high-grade Lion deposit while determining how Nisk Main could potentially contribute to a future development scenario. Power Metallic said new metallurgical studies for Nisk Main are expected before year-end, while drilling at the Lion Deeps extension and environmental and community engagement programs are continuing in parallel.
The Sprott View on Rare Earths and Robotics
According to Sprott's October 2026 report, robotics installations have more than doubled over the past decade as automation expands across manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, defense, and consumer applications. The report cites International Federation of Robotics data showing that the global operational stock of industrial robots reached 4.6 million units at the end of 2024, with more than 500,000 additional units being installed annually.
Rare earth elements are critical for high-performance permanent magnets, sensing systems, displays, and electronics that enable precise robotic movement and efficiency. Sprott cites estimates that advanced industrial and humanoid robots could contain 2-4 kilograms of neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) permanent magnets, which are used in motors, actuators, and precision-control systems.
The potential demand growth extends beyond traditional industrial automation. Goldman Sachs Research has projected the humanoid robot market could reach approximately US$38 billion by 2035, up from roughly US$3 billion. Sprott also cites research suggesting that the increasing complexity of humanoid robots could increase their use of rare-earth-intensive components.
The supply side is another consideration. Sprott notes that China accounted for 91% of global refined output of magnet rare earths and 94% of sintered permanent magnet production in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency. That concentration has increased interest in developing supply chains outside China as governments and manufacturers seek greater access to critical materials.
For investors in the broader critical-materials sector, the connection between robotics and rare earths is therefore primarily a long-term demand and supply-chain story. Power Metallic's Nisk project is not a rare earth project, but its exposure to copper, nickel, palladium, platinum, gold, and silver places it within the broader critical minerals development landscape.
Power Metallic Mines' Nisk Project Update
Power Metallic's September 8, 2026, Mineral Resource Estimate (MRE) established a maiden resource for the Lion Zone of 4.145 million indicated tonnes grading 3.86% copper equivalent (CuEq), plus 0.601 million inferred tonnes grading 4.01% CuEq. More than 85% of the Lion resource is classified as Indicated. The resource contains copper, palladium, platinum, gold, silver, and nickel, with the Indicated portion averaging 1.68% copper before the additional metals are included in the CuEq calculation.
The resource is divided between open-pit and underground portions. The Indicated open-pit component contains approximately 2.782 million tonnes grading 3.45% CuEq, while the Indicated underground portion contains approximately 1.363 million tonnes grading 4.71% CuEq, according to the company's Nisk project resource data. The resource begins at surface and was modeled to more than 600 m (meters) of vertical depth, with mineralization remaining open at depth.
The updated Nisk Main resource stands at 2.703 million indicated tonnes and 2.016 million inferred tonnes, primarily representing nickel-copper mineralization with cobalt and platinum group elements. Power Metallic has said the PEA will focus primarily on Lion while evaluating the appropriate role for Nisk Main as metallurgical work progresses.
The project also has infrastructure that could factor into the eventual development assessment. Power Metallic's Nisk property is located along the Route du Nord in Quebec's James Bay region, with the Albanel Hydro-Québec substation approximately 4 km (kilometers) from Nisk Main and 9.1 km from Lion. The project is also located approximately 30 km from the Nemiscau airport. These existing infrastructure connections are among the factors that will be evaluated as part of the PEA's infrastructure and development planning. Drilling has continued beyond the resource estimate's April 19, 2026, data cutoff.
Noble maintained an "Outperform" rating and US$2.65 price target.
On September 22, Power Metallic reported that hole PML-26-125 intersected 5.70 m grading 14.00% recovery-adjusted CuEq at a vertical depth of nearly 800 m. The result extended the Lion drilling approximately 150 m below the company's previous deepest reported hole and provided additional evidence of mineralization below the current resource. The drilling update reported that the intercept included massive to semi-massive copper sulphides.
The PEA will use the September resource as its basis for mine design and economic analysis, while post-resource drilling results will be reviewed with SGS and BBA as the study advances and may inform future resource updates and subsequent study stages. Power Metallic said the PEA's resource section could accommodate potential future resource growth, although the company has not yet selected an initial development configuration.
Beyond the engineering work, Power Metallic is advancing environmental and community programs. articles.summary: Critical minerals added $26.3 billion to Canada’s economy in 2024, Statistics Canada reports  The Hub | More Signal. Less Noise.

source_detail.name: The Hub | More Signal. Less Noise.

articles.full_text:
Critical mineral production contributed $26.3 billion to Canada’s economy in 2024, about 0.9 percent of nominal GDP and a third of the mining sector’s output, while supporting nearly 57,500 jobs, Statistics Canada said in an Oct. 8 release. The agency cautioned, however, that most of the sector’s headline gains since 2019 trace to volatile commodity prices led by potash rather than to production volumes, which have barely grown.
The numbers arrive as Ottawa courts foreign partners for the minerals that go into batteries, semiconductors and defence systems. Statistics Canada framed the result as evidence of Canada’s position in global supply chains as demand climbs. Real output rose 8.2 percent in 2024, but over the five years from 2019 the volume produced grew only 2.3 percent even as nominal critical mineral GDP jumped 42.3 percent—a gap the agency attributed to price swings that peaked in 2022.
Potash was again the single largest contributor at $7.0 billion, though that is well below its 2022 peak of $14.7 billion after prices partly corrected in 2023. The group Ottawa has designated as prioritized critical minerals—lithium, graphite, nickel, cobalt, copper and rare-earth elements—produced $6.6 billion, and aluminum generated $6.4 billion, the same three categories that have led the sector since 2019. Rounding out the total were $3.1 billion from the service firms that support mining operations and $2.6 billion from a residual category that takes in uranium, helium and zinc.
Growth broadens across every category
After slipping 0.8 percent in 2023, real output grew in every grouping in 2024. Platinum group metals posted the strongest gain at 16.7 percent, with unrefined prioritized minerals up 13.9 percent, refined prioritized minerals up 9.9 percent and support services up 8.6 percent. Employment linked to the sector climbed 5.4 percent to 57,473.

articles.title: How AI-Powered War Drives the Critical Minerals Race - Global Issues.Org
articles.summary: How AI-Powered War Drives the Critical Minerals Race  Global Issues.Org
articles.full_text:
UNITED NATIONS, October 8 (IPS) - The demand for critical minerals is accelerating as world powers scramble to stay on top of emerging technologies. Meanwhile, the environment and frontline communities are paying a steep price.
Such was the basis of the discussion held by the Oakland Institute on September 30, during their webinar: ‘How War and AI Fuel the Critical Minerals Race‘. The event convened experts and frontline activists to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) drives mineral extraction, transforms war technologies, and affects communities entrenched in protracted conflict.
Building on the Institute’s July report, RUSH: Global Scramble for Minerals Wages War on People and Planet, the event highlighted the correlation between rising military spending and the proliferation of AI systems. Panelists stressed that as the demand for critical minerals reaches new peaks, frontline communities bear the brunt of adverse environmental and social impacts.
Anuradha Mittal, founder and Executive Director of the Oakland Institute, noted that military operations account for less than 10 percent of total critical mineral use. Despite this, she warned that the global AI “boom” and increasing competition between world powers over strategic supply chains could trigger a sharp rise in extraction.
Expanding data centers will demand increasingly higher quantities of critical minerals, including copper, gallium, indium, palladium, magnesium, tungsten, germanium, and tantalum. Mittal projected that by 2030, data centers could require an additional 512,000 tons of copper, alongside a 37 percent increase in germanium and an 85 percent increase in gallium by 2033.
She highlighted the United States military-industrial complex as a specific area of concern, describing it as an “AI-first warfighting force.” Under the Trump administration’s proposed 2027 defense budget, military spending would reach a record high of 1.5 trillion USD, nearly twice that of 2023. As the U.S. races to counter China’s dominance across global supply chains, extraction, and processing, the Trump administration has enacted rapid measures to secure minerals internationally.
“Since 2025, the (Trump) administration claims to have signed 38 mineral agreements with countries ranging from Ukraine, India, the DRC, the Philippines, UAE, Australia, Argentina, and Saudi Arabia…Competition with China is bolstering this strategy,” said Mittal. “The Department of War has allocated 75 billion USD to AI-driven programs and another 9 billion to data centers, while the Pentagon requested 13.4 billion dollars in 2026 for autonomous systems. This has driven the U.S. to start stockpiling minerals as strategic assets.”
Other panelists detailed how the impacts of the critical minerals race extend far beyond the global scramble for resources. Frontline communities are not only subjected to environmental degradation, but those in conflict zones are routinely exploited by tech and defense corporations as testing sites for novel military technologies before they are introduced to global markets.
Leila, representing the U.S.-based and Palestinian-led advocacy group Adalah Justice Project (AJP), warned that Gaza has served as an “enormous blueprint for AI-powered war,” noting that Israeli companies have historically used the enclave to test emerging technologies relating to surveillance.
“We have facial recognition drones, different kinds of spyware companies that can hack into phones, and all kinds of AI-assisted targeting programs that, of course, we really learned about through the last couple of years in the genocide,” said Leila. “These tools were developed and tested by Israeli companies in real time, and then sold to the world as sort of ‘battle-proven.’”
Leila also stressed the urgency of the Deadly Merger, a legislative proposal in the U.S. National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) to expand the integration of the U.S. and Israel’s military technology, intelligence, and surveillance systems. AJP posits that the Merger could intensify violence against Palestinians, drive heightened surveillance in the U.S., and impose a “new techno-fascist world order.”
Katerina Canyon, Executive Director of Peace Economy Project—a non-profit organization that advocates for the redirection of military spending toward human needs—introduced the concept of a “peace economy”, where critical resources are used to strengthen healthcare and social infrastructure rather than fund military operations.
Canyon stated that rare earths, lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, and other critical minerals are not only necessities for the proliferation of AI but also are cornerstone resources for the green energy transition. She emphasized that a peace economy must prioritize an equitable environment for civilians over military defensives.
“For nearly fifty years, our organization has challenged militarism and asked what would happen if public resources were directed toward human needs rather than preparation for war,” said Canyon. “My core argument is simple: critical minerals are not politically neutral. The same mineral can become part of a wind turbine, an electric bus, a medical device, or a missile guidance system. Geology does not make that distinction; policy does, government budgets do, procurement decisions do, and industrial strategy does.”
“So the real question is not simply whether we need critical minerals; it is what kind of economy are we building around them,” she continued. “A peace economy starts with a different definition of security. One centered on whether people have safe communities, have healthcare, clean energy, transportation, housing, and a livable environment.”

articles.title: Vijay Prashad: Critical Minerals & the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ - Consortium News
articles.summary: Vijay Prashad: Critical Minerals & the ‘Donroe Doctrine’  Consortium News
articles.full_text:
The U.S. wants to reorganise the mineral wealth of the Western Hemisphere around its own industrial and military needs while keeping China at arm’s length.
By Vijay Prashad
Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research
The map of the new war over minerals stretches from the lithium flats of South America to the rare-earth deposits of Greenland. Its vocabulary is familiar: supply-chain resilience, national security, diversification and partnership.
Beneath these neutral phrases lies an older project.
The United States wants to reorganise the mineral wealth of the Western Hemisphere around its own industrial and military needs while keeping China at arm’s length. The latest name for this ambition is President Donald Trump’s Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine of 1823 — crudely nicknamed the “Donroe Doctrine.” The joke is crude, but the politics are not.
Critical minerals are not inherently critical. Copper, lithium, graphite, cobalt, nickel and rare earths become critical within a particular system of production that increasingly requires electrical grids, batteries, data centres, semiconductors, satellites and fighter aircraft.
The International Energy Agency expects demand for these minerals to almost double by 2040 under stated policies, with lithium demand more than tripling. The decisive bottleneck is not geology but the command of metallurgy, patents, finance, separating, refining and markets. China refines more than 90 percent of global gallium, graphite, manganese and several key categories of rare earths. This is the industrial fact that Washington’s security documents translate into the language of “threat.”
In April 2025, the White House ordered a Section 232 investigation into processed critical minerals and their derivative products, treating import dependence as a possible threat to national security.
In January 2026, after the investigation concluded that such imports did threaten U.S. security, Trump directed negotiations with trading partners and proposed price floors and other trade restrictions.
In July, he invoked the Defense Production Act for the recovery of critical minerals from scrap and used goods. Taken together, these measures by the United States government describe a belligerent industrial policy that is backed by tariffs and military threats.
U.S. critical minerals policy is designed not only to seek mines abroad but also to enforce political authority over where these minerals may be sold, whose technology may process them and which banks may finance the chain.
The 2025 Trump executive order on seabed minerals stated its objective with unusual clarity: the United States will strengthen “partnerships with allies and industry to counter China’s growing influence over seabed mineral resources.”
The Trump Corollary extends that logic across the hemisphere, treating Latin America and the Caribbean not as a region of sovereign development projects but as the near abroad of the United States: a protected reservoir of agricultural commodities, metals, minerals, ports and sea-lanes.
In his monumental book Open Veins of Latin America (1971), Eduardo Galeano wrote of the “mortality of wealth” — how the region’s natural abundance brought sorrow to its peoples. This ugly contradiction between wealth and exploitation continues.
Greenland reveals the Trump Corollary in its most naked form. Far from an empty white space as it is often portrayed, this Inuit society of roughly 57,000 people has a long history of Danish colonial rule and an unfinished struggle for self-determination. Its position between North America and Europe, the U.S. military base at Pituffik, the opening Arctic sea routes and deposits that include rare-earth minerals have made it an object of renewed attention.
Trump’s repeated desire to acquire Greenland reduces the Inuit people’s homeland to real estate and military strategy. Trump claims that he has now taken Greenland from Denmark, but the details of the security agreement are far more ambiguous than his social media posts.
The pressure on Greenland and on Latin America is part of the same imperial imagination. The U.S. sees the former as its northern shield and the latter as its southern storehouse.
In both, the stated aim is to prevent Chinese capital, infrastructure and technology from gaining a durable position. Yet what is at stake is not the freedom of Chinese investment but the sovereignty of countries to chart their own independent foreign and economic policy. The issue is that Washington claims the authority to decide which relationships are permissible. The promise of sovereignty becomes conditional on alignment with U.S. imperial ambitions.
Latin America has lived through this story. Galeano’s book details the journey of silver from Bolivia, guano from Peru, nitrates from Chile, copper from Chile and Peru, iron ore from Brazil and oil from Venezuela to successive centres of capitalist accumulation.
The commodity changes from country to country but the structure endures: extraction at the periphery, technology and finance elsewhere and socialised damage at the pithead. The so-called green transition can repaint this structure without overturning it.
The figures reveal both the opportunity and the danger. The International Energy Agency reports that, excluding lithium, Latin American countries refined on average only 20 percent of the key energy minerals they extracted in 2025. Under the existing project pipeline, the region could capture about $185 billion in economic value by 2035, but only one-fifth would come from refining. Greater local refining could raise that value to roughly $220 billion.
The U.N. Conference on Trade and Development argues for a regional industrial policy with greater public investment in infrastructure and education, clear rules for locally sourced goods and labour (local-content rules) and technology transfer and control over the pace and terms of extraction. The question is whether these tools will serve public planning or merely subsidise foreign corporations.
The epicentre of this debate is Brazil, which holds about 23 percent of known rare-earth reserves but produces roughly 1 percent of global output and lacks an integrated processing chain that runs from separation through metal and alloy production to permanent magnet manufacturing.
At the Pela Ema mine in Goiás, the Serra Verde Group produces a mixed rare-earth carbonate. The difficult and profitable stages take place abroad. Brazil keeps the excavation, some jobs and taxes and the environmental liabilities while higher-value production, patents and strategic control leave the country.
This is why the proposed acquisition of Serra Verde by U.S.-backed USA Rare Earth matters. The deposit contains dysprosium and terbium, indispensable for high-performance magnets used in electric motors and military systems. U.S. financing and purchase commitments turn the acquisition into more than a private transaction: it is part of a state-directed attempt to construct a supply chain that excludes China. Around the mine, rural and quilombola communities face polluted streams, threats to their land and mining claims that menace agrarian-reform settlements. A mineral cannot be called “green” when its costs are transferred to the people who live above it.
Brazil’s answer cannot be a simple change of customer. Cooperation with China, the United States, or Europe should be judged by what knowledge and capacity remain in Brazil, not by the nationality of the buyer. Certain basic rules must apply:
- Public control over geological information and strategic deposits.
- Public finance through the Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES).
- Public investigation of the ecological impact, including environmental licensing to examine cumulative watershed impacts.
- Indigenous, quilombola and local agrarian communities must have enforceable rights to free, prior, and informed consultation.
- Scrutiny of foreign takeovers of mines.
- Technology transfer requirements written into contracts.
- Research led by Brazilian universities and public research institutes.
- Mandatory domestic separation and refining of the ore.
- Regional cooperation to build scale in batteries, chemicals, machinery, magnets and recycling.
The countries of the South must reject the false choice between serving a Chinese-centred chain and entering a U.S.-controlled one. Social movements must fight for popular sovereignty, which would require that these arrangements be made with public companies, through public institutions, with transparent mandates, common environmental standards, and shared research. The extraction of metals and minerals must be planned for socially necessary uses and not by the dictates of luxury consumption and permanent war.
The deepest vulnerability exposed by the mineral contest is not dependence on one country. It is the subordination of life to supply chains governed elsewhere.
The Trump Corollary promises to secure the hemisphere and its wealth for the United States. A people’s doctrine would secure natural resources for the benefit of those who live on the land, prioritising electricity before exports, water before waste, knowledge before royalties, and sovereignty before alignment.
The wealth beneath the soil must become visible in schools, hospitals, research centres, laboratories, restored ecosystems, and dignified lives — a future that cannot be shipped away in sacks of concentrate.
In 1904, the Nicaraguan poet Rubén Darío wrote “A Roosevelt (To Roosevelt).” Addressed to U.S. President Theodore Roosevelt, the poem is a powerful indictment of imperialismo yanqui (Yankee imperialism). The stanzas below allude to Victor Hugo’s 1872 “Le Message de Grant” (Grant’s Message), in which Hugo writes to U.S. President Ulysses S. Grant that the U.S. flag, “sown with stars,” is “obscured” with a “stain of mud” (tache de boue):
| Los Estados Unidos son potentes y grandes. Cuando ellos se estremecen hay un hondo temblor que pasa

Highlights
- Freeport operates some of the world's most economically viable and geologically significant copper mines, including Grasberg in Indonesia and operations across Arizona, Peru, and Congo.
- The company's molybdenum and gold production from copper mining operations provide important revenue diversification and geological realitythese metals come out of the ground alongside copper rather.
- Capital allocation decisions around mine expansion, environmental remediation, and shareholder returns reflect the company's navigation of a cyclical commodity industry while managing long-dated mine.
Freeport-McMoRan Inc (NYSE/TSX:FCX) stands as one of the world's largest integrated copper producers, with significant exposure to molybdenum and gold as valuable by-products. As global supply chains tighten and the electric vehicle revolution demands unprecedented quantities of copper, Freeport's diverse portfolio of operating minesspanning North America, South America, and Indonesiapositions the company at the centre of commodity market dynamics. The company's ability to navigate mine permitting challenges, capital intensity requirements, and geopolitical complexities while maintaining production efficiency continues to shape investor interest in the metals and mining sector. Investors following Metal and Mining Stocks can track Freeport-McMoRan Inc (TSX:FCX) FCX (TSX:FCX) against the S&P/TSX Composite Index (TXCX) as a benchmark for the wider market.
The Global Copper Imperative and Freeport's Market Position
Copper serves as the nervous system of modern civilization. It conducts electricity in power distribution networks, telephone lines, and computer circuits. It alloys with other metals to create brass and bronze, essential materials for countless industrial applications. Most critically for current market dynamics, copper forms the electrical backbone of electric vehicle charging infrastructure and renewable energy systems. As governments worldwide commit to decarbonization targets and the transportation sector transitions from internal combustion engines to battery-electric propulsion, copper demand faces structural growth that extends beyond typical commodity cycles.
Freeport-McMoRan occupies a unique position within this landscape. The company operates integrated mining operations that generate copper as the primary product, with molybdenum and gold emerging naturally from the geological and metallurgical realities of the deposit architecture. This integrated approach means Freeport's business model responds directly to the copper supercycle that many analysts identify as fundamental to the next decade of commodity market dynamics.
The company's Indonesian operations, centered on the Grasberg mine, represent one of the world's most significant copper resources. Grasberg's geological endowment consists of porphyry copper depositslarge, disseminated ore bodies containing moderate concentrations of copper across expansive volumes of rock. These deposits require volume processing rather than selective high-grade mining, making them economically viable at specific copper price points while generating substantial annual production volumes that flow into global supply chains.
Mining Operations and Geographic Diversification
Freeport's operating footprint spans continents, creating both opportunities and complexities. The company's North American operations center on mines in Arizona, where deposits include the Morenci, Bagdad, and Safford mines. These operations demonstrate the company's ability to maintain production from conventional open-pit mining in a developed jurisdictional environment with established regulatory frameworks. The Arizona portfolio benefits from proximity to infrastructure, skilled labour, and supply chains, though operating within environmentally conscious jurisdictions means adherence to rigorous permitting and monitoring standards.
The Peru operations, particularly around the Cerro Verde mine and exploration properties, expose Freeport to South America's geological potential alongside the region's particular regulatory and political complexities. Peru ranks among the world's top copper-producing nations, and the country's mining sector generates substantial government revenue and employment. This dependency creates powerful political incentives for mining to continue, though community engagement, environmental standards, and regional disputes over water resources and land access create ongoing operational challenges that affect mining expansion and mine life extension projects.
The Grasberg operation in Indonesia represents the company's most geologically endowed asset. The mine sits within the Pangkoh deposit complex, which geological surveys indicate contains copper resources measured in hundreds of millions of tonnes. The transition from underground mining at Grasberg to deeper underground operations, following the depletion of accessible open-pit material, illustrates the long-term trajectory of major mines as mining engineers must eventually descend deeper into the earth to maintain production.
Key Commodities and Molybdenum's Value
While copper dominates Freeport's revenue and marketing narrative, the company's mines produce molybdenum in concentrations that reflect the geological characteristics of porphyry copper deposits. Molybdenum functions as a refractory metal with critical applications in high-strength steels, where it improves toughness and wear resistance, and in catalysts for petroleum refining, where molybdenum compounds facilitate the conversion of crude oil into usable products. These applications mean molybdenum demand correlates with industrial production and petroleum refining activity, creating price cycles that often move independently from copper.
Freeport's molybdenum production exists within the broader competitive landscape of molybdenum supply, where the metal emerges as a by-product from copper mining at Freeport but represents a primary mining focus for competitors like Centerra Gold and Climax Molybdenum. The supply-demand dynamics for molybdenum reflect long investment cycles in refinery infrastructure and catalysts, making the market responsive to industrial activity and petroleum pricing.
Gold production from Freeport's operations represents another valuable by-product stream. The company's copper mines generate gold at concentrations and recovery rates determined by the mineralogy of specific deposits rather than gold-focused extraction strategies. This means Freeport's gold production fluctuates with mining volumes and geological characteristics rather than following a dedicated gold mining strategy. However, the gold revenue stream provides important earnings diversification when copper prices face headwinds.
Geographical Footprint and Reserve Base
Freeport's reserve base consists of measurable geological resourcesportions of ore bodies where the company has drilled sufficient holes to estimate metal content with reasonable geological confidence. The company's Grasberg deposit remains among the world's largest and longest-lived copper reserves, with geological studies suggesting decades of mineable material remaining. This reserve longevity provides confidence in production continuity and long-dated cash flow visibility, factors that underpin investor confidence in the company's dividending capacity and capital investment programs.
The reserve base at Grasberg and other major operations reflects the geological reality that porphyry copper deposits contain substantial volumes of lower-grade ore. The economically mineable portion depends on copper prices, mining costs, and processing efficiency. When copper prices rise, operators can mine lower-grade material profitably. When prices decline, mining shifts toward higher-grade zones or pauses entirely if prices fall below marginal production costs.
Production Efficiency and Cost Structure
Freeport's production efficiency depends on several interconnected factors: ore grade at individual mines, processing technology and capacity, labour productivity, and energy costs. The company's different operations exhibit different cost structures reflecting their geological, geographical, and technical characteristics.
The Arizona operations, despite lower ore grades and higher labour costs than some emerging market competitors, benefit from established mining infrastructure, reliable electricity supply, and predictable operating environments. The company has invested substantially in processing plant optimization and environmental control systems, reflecting both regulatory requirements and competitive positioning in the North American market.
The Peru operations reflect South American characteristicslower labour costs than North America but more volatile operating environments and greater community engagement requirements. Water availability, particularly crucial for copper ore processing, requires careful management in Peru's arid regions.
Grasberg's cost structure reflects the mine's exceptional ore grades and the company's large-scale, long-lived operation. The massive scale allows for specialized equipment and processing systems optimized for the specific geological and metallurgical characteristics of the deposit.

articles.full_text:
Patna: Bihar is preparing a major investment push in the energy sector, with proposed projects worth around ₹1,88,383 crore across power generation, energy storage, transmission, distribution and renewable energy.
The plans come as the state’s peak electricity demand is projected to reach 11,747 MW by 2030, compared with around 9,475 MW currently. Energy Secretary and BSPHCL CMD Ajay Yadav shared the details at an India Energy Week (IEW) 2027 awareness programme at IIT Patna.
Bihar’s Power Demand Continues to Rise
Bihar now has around 2.32 crore electricity consumers. The state’s maximum power demand has risen from about 2,831 MW in 2014 to around 9,475 MW, creating the need for large-scale expansion of its energy infrastructure.
The state is targeting 24 GW of renewable energy capacity and 6.1 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2029-30. Its Renewable Energy Policy-2025 also provides incentives to attract investment and promote clean-energy projects.
Read also: A New Way to Give Back: Bihar to Expand “Danveer” Asset Donation Drive
₹1.32 Lakh Crore for Generation and Storage
Around ₹1,32,521 crore of the proposed investment is earmarked for power generation and energy storage projects.
A major component is the planned development of around 8,400 MW of pumped storage capacity across Nawada, Jamui, Banka and Munger under Bihar’s Pumped Storage Project Policy-2025.
Other major projects include:
- A 1,100 MW rooftop solar programme for around 10 lakh Kutir Jyoti consumers under PM Surya Ghar Yojana.
- 500 MW grid-connected rooftop solar capacity on government buildings.
- A 150 MW Aurangabad solar park with battery storage.
- A proposed 4×700 MW nuclear power project in Banka.
₹1,040 Crore Push for Green Hydrogen
Bihar is also preparing to build a green hydrogen ecosystem following Cabinet approval of its Green Hydrogen Policy.
The initiative carries a provision of around ₹1,040 crore and will initially focus on developing five Green Hydrogen Villages on a pilot basis.
The villages will explore the use of green hydrogen for clean cooking and electricity generation. Each selected village will receive an incentive of ₹1 crore, creating a local demonstration model for clean-energy adoption.
Transmission and Distribution Get Major Investments
The state also plans substantial spending to strengthen the electricity network.
Around ₹24,683 crore is proposed for the transmission sector, which will support the development of 56 new substations and nearly 7,400 circuit kilometres of transmission lines.
Another ₹28,809 crore is proposed for expansion and modernisation of the distribution network. In addition, around ₹2,370 crore is planned for maintenance and digital infrastructure.
These investments are expected to improve the capacity and reliability of Bihar’s electricity network as demand continues to grow.
Smart and Cleaner Energy Future
Beyond physical infrastructure, Bihar is also focusing on smart metering, energy efficiency, electric vehicles, rooftop solar and clean energy. The broader approach aims to make the state’s power system more efficient, secure and capable of handling rising consumption.
The proposed investments also position renewable energy and storage as important parts of Bihar’s future power mix, while pumped storage can provide greater flexibility for integrating renewable power into the grid.
IEW 2027 to Showcase Bihar’s Energy Potential
The India Energy Week 2027 platform is being used to present Bihar’s energy-sector achievements, investment opportunities and future projects to national and international stakeholders.
With growing electricity demand and large planned investments in generation, storage, transmission, distribution and renewable energy, Bihar is seeking to build a stronger and more secure energy system. The proposed projects could also create new opportunities for clean-energy investment, technology adoption and regional development across the state.

University of Birmingham Leads £6.2M Project to Develop Protein-Based Membranes for Selective Lithium Extraction
At the University of Birmingham, a research team is heading a three-year effort backed by £6.2 million, equivalent to $8.2 million, to create membranes made from proteins that may allow more selective and possibly lower-energy lithium recovery. Funding comes from the UK's Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA). The first goal is among the hardest problems in direct lithium extraction (DLE): isolating lithium from sodium so that high-purity lithium compounds suitable for battery production can be obtained.
Dr. Dominik Kubicki, who leads the project at the University of Birmingham, explained that ordered materials can be built by biology with a level of precision that current manufacturing approaches struggle to match. The team intends to use that capability to produce membranes whose pores are uniform and programmable. Beyond battery materials, the technology might later be applied to critical-mineral recovery, water treatment, and chemical and pharmaceutical manufacturing. Whether it succeeds will hinge on turning the exactness of biological structures into robust membranes that can function at industrial scale.
Protein engineering
Aston University and three industry partners form the consortium behind the work. It plans to employ S-layer proteins, which on the surfaces of many microorganisms naturally form highly ordered two-dimensional lattices. The researchers want to modify these proteins into large-area membranes with pores of a consistent size that can tell lithium ions apart from sodium ions even though the two have similar chemical behaviour.
The effort sits within ARIA's Universal Fabricators programme, which aims to treat engineered proteins as programmable components for making materials with unusually precise control over their geometry. Professor Tim Knowles, a co-lead on the project, described S-layer proteins as an exceptional foundation for materials engineering because they self-assemble into highly ordered arrangements. He added that computational design, structural biology and experimental screening will be brought together in an attempt to reprogram these natural components for demanding technological tasks.
Expertise from industry will support various stages of development. AI-guided protein design will be directed by Jude Wells of Fold9. Membrane manufacturing, scale-up and testing will be carried out by Evove, a UK-based company. Adaptyv Bio will supply high-throughput screening to assess thousands of protein variants. Candidates showing the most promise will be produced at larger scale and incorporated into working membrane systems.
Scaling challenges
Computational protein design, structural biology and high-throughput screening will be paired with protein production, membrane production and testing under conditions resembling real operations. Professor Owen Thomas of the University of Birmingham noted that a major difficulty will be moving from molecular-level control to membranes that can be made and run at useful scales. According to him, tightly linking biological design, materials characterisation and chemical engineering allows the team to tackle that difficulty from the start.
The programme will also combine computational protein design, structural biology and experimental screening with membrane production and testing under realistic operating conditions. While the approach is still at the research stage, the consortium hopes to build a manufacturing platform that can yield highly selective separation materials for several industries. For lithium producers, the decisive question will be whether the engineered membranes can provide dependable separation performance beyond the lab while retaining the durability and scalability required for commercial deployment.

An overview of socio-environmental governance of the sector
This case study is part of a broader project focused on strengthening supply chain resilience through analysis of the environmental and associated social impacts of critical minerals using case studies of nickel, lithium, and copper. It examines the environmental challenges and associated social issues arising from both industrial and artisanal copper mining in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
Key Messages
- The concentration and expansion of mining activities, particularly in the Copperbelt, have created pressures on land, water, air quality, biodiversity, and communities, and in many cases interact with longer-standing challenges related to urbanization, infrastructure, and poverty.
- Environmental monitoring, cumulative impact assessment, management of legacy mine sites, enforcement, effective application of community and artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) provisions, and the monitoring and enforcement of child labour regulations remain critical areas for attention.
- Strengthening capacity, improving environmental data, clarifying responsibility for historical and cumulative impacts, and supporting implementation of existing requirements could reduce environmental and social risks and boost the contribution of copper and cobalt mining to sustainable development.
- The DRC’s Mining Code and its implementing regulations establish requirements relating to environmental assessment and management, mine rehabilitation and closure, community consultation and development, compensation and resettlement, local content, and formalization of ASM.
In 2025, the DRC produced 3.2 million metric tons of copper, making it the world’s second largest copper producer. Copper and cobalt mining is central to the DRC’s economy and to global mineral supply chains, while also supporting a wide range of livelihoods through both large-scale mining and ASM.
At the same time, the concentration and expansion of mining activities, particularly in the Copperbelt, have created significant pressures on land, water, air quality, biodiversity, and surrounding communities. These impacts vary considerably between locations and types of mining, and in many cases interact with longer-standing challenges related to urbanization, infrastructure, poverty, and historical mining activity.
The conclusions and lessons learned from this case study can inform sustainable approaches to copper mining and processing in the DRC as well as other jurisdictions.

articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Glencore's business model combines mining, smelting, and commodity trading, generating revenue from both physical commodity production and trading value-added activitiesa structure that diversifies.
- The company produces copper, zinc, nickel, cobalt, and other metals essential to electrification and battery technology.
- Geographic diversification across Africa (major cobalt and copper production), Australia (zinc and copper), Latin America (copper).
Glencore plc (LSE:GLEN / TSX:GLEN) operates as one of the world's largest diversified mining and commodity trading companies, generating revenue from copper, zinc, coal, oil, agricultural commodities, and other materials. The company's integrated business modelcombining mining operations with marketing and trading functionscreates multiple revenue streams and allows the company to capture value across commodity supply chains. With operations spanning Africa, Australia, South America, and Asia, and trading operations extending globally, Glencore's portfolio reflects both the investment opportunities and transitional challenges facing diversified commodity producers in an era of energy transition and climate policy evolution. Within Metal and Mining Stocks, movements in the S&P/TSX Composite Index (TXCX) provide helpful context for how Glencore plc (TSX:GLEN) GLEN (TSX:GLEN) is performing relative to its peers.
Glencore's Integrated Commodity Business Model
Glencore's distinctive business model separates the company from many competitors. While most mining companies focus primarily on extracting and selling raw materials, Glencore operates along multiple points in commodity value chains. The company mines copper, zinc, and nickel. It operates smelting and refining facilities that process concentrates into refined metals traded on global exchanges. It maintains marketing operations that work with customers to optimize their commodity procurement. And it operates a substantial trading division that takes positions in commodity markets, hedges price exposure, and captures opportunities from price movements across different commodity markets and geographic locations.
This integrated approach means Glencore's profitability reflects not only commodity production volumes and prices but also the company's ability to add value through processing, marketing, and trading activities. During periods when mining margins compress due to declining commodity prices or rising production costs, trading and marketing operations can generate offsetting profits. Conversely, when mining profits expand due to rising commodity prices, the company may reduce trading exposure to deleverage and preserve capital.
Copper Production and the Energy Transition Narrative
Glencore's copper production derives from several major operations. The Katanga mining complex in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) ranks among the world's largest copper producers. Copper mines in Australia, particularly the Cobar operation and Copper Mountain operations, contribute additional volumes. The company's Peruvian operations, through various joint ventures and owned properties, add to the copper portfolio. Combined, Glencore produces tens of thousands of tonnes of copper annually from a geographically diverse portfolio.
Copper's fundamental role in electrical systems, power transmission, and renewable energy infrastructure creates a compelling long-term demand narrative. As electricity grids expand, solar and wind installations proliferate, and electric vehicle adoption accelerates, copper demand should sustain at elevated levels relative to historical norms. Glencore's copper portfolio therefore sits at the intersection of this structural demand growth.
However, copper prices fluctuate substantially around this underlying trend line. Global economic slowdowns compress demand. Competing production from other miners responds to prices, creating cyclic supply dynamics. China, which historically drove copper demand growth but now faces slowing economic growth and manufacturing headwinds, influences global copper markets significantly. Glencore's copper operations thus exhibit high sensitivity to global economic conditions and Chinese industrial activity.
Zinc: Industrial Metal Facing Cyclical Challenges
Zinc serves as a corrosion-resistant coating applied to steel surfaces, protecting infrastructure from rust and deterioration. Zinc alloys with copper to create brass, essential for plumbing fixtures and industrial applications. Zinc oxide finds applications in rubber manufacturing, pharmaceutical compounds, and numerous industrial processes. Global zinc demand therefore correlates with construction activity, automotive production, and general industrial output.
Glencore operates significant zinc assets, including the Mopani mines in Zambia and Queensland operations in Australia. The company's zinc mines produce substantial annual volumes, positioning Glencore among global zinc market participants. Zinc prices, like copper, fluctuate based on supply-demand dynamics, though zinc cycles often move independently from copper due to distinct demand drivers. When construction activity weakens, zinc demand declines disproportionately. Conversely, strong construction and infrastructure spending elevates zinc prices.
The zinc market faces structural supply challenges. Many zinc mines age and decline in production as ore grades decline. Few new major zinc projects have come online in recent years. This supply tightness suggests long-term price support, though cyclical downturns can still generate short-term pricing pressure.
Nickel, Cobalt, and Battery Metals
Glencore's nickel and cobalt operations position the company within the critical minerals spacemetals essential to battery technology and electrification. Nickel serves as a key cathode material in lithium-ion batteries, with higher-purity nickel enabling higher energy density and longer range in electric vehicles. Cobalt similarly functions as a critical battery ingredient, with applications in both cathode compositions and charging systems.
The company's cobalt operations in the Democratic Republic of Congo generate substantial revenue. DRC produces a significant portion of global cobalt supply, and Glencore's large footprint in the region provides exposure to this critical mineral. Cobalt prices have experienced substantial volatility, reflecting supply concentration risk and demand cycles in battery manufacturing.
Nickel production comes from Glencore's assets in Indonesia and other locations. Nickel markets have evolved substantially as battery demand has grown and traditional stainless steel applications have faced cyclical pressures. High-purity nickel production commands premium prices relative to lower-grade material.
The strategic importance of battery metals means Glencore's nickel and cobalt operations exist within frameworks of government policy, supply security concerns, and environmental scrutiny. Processing and refining these metals involves chemical processes generating environmental considerations. Producing nations have begun implementing policies to benefit from value-added processing within their borders rather than allowing raw ore exports. These factors shape Glencore's operational and strategic challenges.
Coal Exposure and Energy Transition Headwinds
Glencore operates substantial coal mining operations in Australia and other regions. Coal production represents a legacy of the company's historical growth, reflecting the commodity's historical importance as an energy source. Coal pricing responds to electricity demand, global power generation trends, and increasingly, policy restrictions on coal consumption.
The global energy transition poses structural headwinds for coal. Renewable energy costs have declined dramatically, making wind and solar increasingly cost-competitive with coal power. Policy restrictions, ranging from coal plant retirement mandates to carbon taxes, constrain coal demand. Institutional investors increasingly divest from coal companies on environmental, social, and governance grounds.
However, coal remains essential to global electricity generation, particularly in developing economies where coal plants operate and generate electricity at lower capital costs than renewable alternatives. The Galveston Wharves Board of Trustees has approved a lease and development agreement with Power LNG, which paves the way for the first LNG bunkering facility on the Gulf Coast. Power LNG plans to develop a small-scale, modular liquefied natural gas production, storage, and fuel bunkering facility on Pelican Island, with port officials highlighting that the project will position Galveston to serve the growing demand for LNG as a marine fuel both in the port and the region.
The board approved the agreement that provides for a 30-acre greenfield development, which will be located on the east side of an approximately 82-acre, port-owned tract on the deep-water Galveston Harbor. It will be part of the port’s plan for the development of what it highlighted as one of Texas’ few underdeveloped large-scale deepwater port sites. The port owns 357 acres of prime waterfront acreage, including 100 acres on Galveston Harbor adjacent to the Gulf Cooper shipyard, which Davie Defense is developing into a shipbuilding facility for the Arctic icebreakers and other projects.
Power LNG plans to develop an LNG facility capable of producing approximately 400,000 gallons per day. The facility will use two parallel liquefaction trains, each capable of producing about 200,000 gallons per day, with the potential to expand production at this site to 800,000 gallons per day using modular liquefaction technology. Power LNG also proposes to build an underground natural gas pipeline to provide feedstock to the facility, a 3-million-gallon LNG storage tank, and a shore-to-ship pier to fuel both ships and bunker vessels.
Austin Terry, Power LNG CEO, highlighted that the company will develop a fully integrated LNG fueling solution, including liquefaction, storage, bunkering, vessel loading, and export capabilities.
The facility is projected to begin commercial production in the fourth quarter of 2028, following completion of required approvals and agreements. Galveston highlights that Power LNG’s strategic partners and customers are expected to coordinate LNG bunkering operations, which may provide LNG fuel to ships calling at the Port of Galveston and other locations in the Galveston, Houston, and Texas City ship channels.
“As more LNG-powered ships are built, demand for LNG marine fuel is reaching a tipping point,” said Rodger Rees, Galveston Wharves port director and CEO. “This facility will give Galveston an opportunity to support this growing market while further diversifying our port’s operations,” Rees said, predicting this development will pave the way for the Port of Galveston to play a leading role in providing cleaner marine fuels to the region.
