articles.full_text:
A $240 million liquefied natural gas production and fueling facility planned for Pelican Island moved closer to reality Thursday when the Wharves Board of Trustees approved a lease and development agreement with Power LNG Ventures.
The project, known as Project Seawolf, would establish what developers describe as the Gulf Coast’s first fully integrated marine LNG fueling facility, providing fuel for cruise ships and cargo vessels operating in the Galveston, Houston and Texas City ship channels.
The agreement follows a unanimous July vote approving a preliminary term sheet that allowed port officials to negotiate a long-term lease for about 30 acres of port-owned property on Pelican Island.
At the time, the trustees, who govern the public port, emphasized that several questions remained about safety, the facility’s footprint and future waterfront access.
Thursday’s unanimous approval advances the project beyond those preliminary negotiations, although construction remains contingent on financing, regulatory permits and other development requirements, the parties said.
Under the agreement, Power LNG will lease about 30 acres of port-owned property for an initial 30-year term, with options for two 10-year renewals, according to lease documents.
The company will pay $62,500 in monthly base rent, increasing to $100,000 if production capacity exceeds 440,000 gallons a day, along with a fee of 1 cent for every gallon of LNG produced.
At the facility’s planned initial production capacity of 400,000 gallons daily, the agreement could generate about $2.21 million annually for the port, assuming year-round production, before additional charges and annual rent increases.
Power LNG also is responsible for financing, permitting, constructing and operating the facility.
Power LNG plans to invest about $240 million in the initial development, which would produce 400,000 gallons of LNG daily through two liquefaction units, officials said.
Liquefied natural gas is a super-cooled form of natural gas, primarily composed of methane, used as a fuel.
The facility would include a 3-million-gallon storage tank, underground natural gas pipeline and pier capable of loading LNG directly onto ships and specialized bunkering vessels.
Production could eventually double to 800,000 gallons daily, with storage capacity expanding to 6 million gallons.
The project is expected to create about 25 permanent jobs and another 30 full-time-equivalent contract positions, along with construction and waterfront labor opportunities, according to company documents.
“This agreement paves the way for the Port of Galveston to play a leading role in providing cleaner marine fuels to the region,” Port Director and CEO Rodger Rees said. “The project will create jobs, bring more LNG-powered ships and contribute to improved air quality.”
LNG fueled vessels emit lower levels of carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides and sulfur oxides than those burning traditional marine fuels, advocates say.
The development comes as cruise lines and cargo carriers increasingly adopt LNG-powered vessels.
Power LNG estimates more than 10 LNG-fueled cruise ships could operate from Galveston within the next decade.
The project represents a significant opportunity to expand Galveston’s role in the growing marine LNG market while attracting additional maritime business to the region, Power LNG CEO Austin Terry said.
“The growth of marine LNG creates significant economic opportunity for the Galveston/Houston region while supporting the evolving needs of next-generation vessels and global trade,” Terry said.
The company also proposes an 800,000-gallon storage facility near Pier 38 and LNG exports to Mexico and the Caribbean through specialized containers loaded at Pier 34.
Those export plans represent a broader scope than the marine fueling operation initially emphasized during July’s board discussions.
A federal Department of Energy application previously filed by Power LNG sought authorization to export up to 51.75 billion cubic feet of LNG annually, raising questions about the project’s potential long-term scale.
The proposal also revives a controversial chapter in Pelican Island’s history.
BP abandoned plans for a $600 million LNG import terminal in 2006 amid changing market conditions and local opposition. Another proposed LNG development involving Next Decade ultimately fell through after the company shifted its focus to Brownsville.
During July’s discussions, trustees raised concerns about the proposed facility’s safety, potential blast radius and whether the port would retain control of future waterfront operations.
LNG itself does not burn in liquid form, but escaping gas can create a flammable vapor cloud under certain conditions.
Power LNG’s development schedule anticipates equipment orders beginning in early 2027, with commercial production targeted for the fourth quarter of 2028.
The company must still secure necessary permits and financing before construction can proceed.

articles.summary: Kinder Morgan Restores U.S.-Mexico Gas Flows After Pipeline Outage  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com

Kinder Morgan has lifted force majeure on its Tennessee Gas Pipeline after repairs restored natural gas deliveries to Mexico that had been interrupted earlier this week.
Tennessee Gas identified problems on October 5 and isolated sections of the system, including the Rio Bravo and Cenagas delivery meters. The company declared force majeure the following day. Kinder Morgan said Thursday that the problems had been resolved and shipments were being restored.
The outage was brief, but Mexico doesn’t have much room for even a brief one.
About 75% of the country’s natural gas comes from Texas, making Mexico the largest buyer of U.S. pipeline gas. American exports south of the border have climbed from roughly 1 billion cubic feet per day in 2010 to around 8 Bcf/d today.
Mexican pipeline operator CENAGAS had been warned that flows could fall by as much as 20% during the outage. Director Cuitlahuac Garcia described the situation as critical.
Mexico has roughly three days of gas reserves, according to Garcia. The country does not have large-scale underground storage comparable to the United States, leaving its power sector heavily dependent on continuous pipeline deliveries from the north.
That dependence has grown along with Mexico’s use of natural gas for electricity generation and industrial demand.
President Claudia Sheinbaum’s government has started exploring limited use of hydraulic fracturing to increase domestic gas production. Mexico is also planning about $8 billion in pipeline investment to strengthen its gas network.
Neither addresses the storage problem quickly.
Tennessee Gas Pipeline moves gas from producing regions in Louisiana, South Texas, the Gulf Coast and Appalachia into markets across the United States, Canada and Mexico. Interruptions on sections feeding the Mexican border can therefore reach far beyond the affected pipe itself.
This week’s outage did not last long enough to create a prolonged supply shortage. It did give Mexico another look at the arithmetic behind its gas system: roughly 8 Bcf/d arriving from the United States, three days of reserve supply, and a grid that cannot afford many interruptions.

Welcome To ChemAnalyst
	Russia Prioritizes Domestic Sulphuric Acid Supply
	Under Government Decree No. 1158, exports of sulphuric acid classified under HS code 2807 00 000 1 require approval from the Russian government based on proposals from the Ministry of Industry and Trade. International transit shipments and certain intergovernmental arrangements are exempt, while other exports require specific authorization. This effectively limits the availability of Russian sulphuric acid in international spot markets during the remainder of the year.
	The decision is particularly significant for fertilizer producers because sulphuric acid is a critical input for producing phosphoric acid, which is subsequently used to manufacture phosphate fertilizers. Any reduction in acid availability can therefore affect fertilizer production economics, especially when sulphur costs are already elevated.
	Sulphur Restrictions Add to the Supply Pressure
	Russia's latest sulphuric acid measure comes alongside a separate restriction on exports of elemental sulphur. Russia has prohibited exports of liquid, granular and lump sulphur through December 31, with limited exemptions, including certain lower-grade sulphur shipments authorized by the Ministry of Industry and Trade.
	This combination is important because sulphur is a major feedstock for sulphuric acid production. Global sulphur markets have already faced significant disruption from Russian export restrictions and constraints on Middle Eastern shipments linked to wider geopolitical and transportation disruptions. A recent agricultural-market analysis reported that the combined impact had removed a substantial portion of internationally traded sulphur from normal availability.
	Fertilizer and Industrial Markets Face Higher Supply Risk
	The restriction could have consequences well beyond Russia's borders. Fertilizer producers in import-dependent markets may need to seek alternative sulphuric acid supplies, potentially increasing competition for cargoes from other producing regions. Higher feedstock and acid costs could also influence phosphate fertilizer production margins.
	The pressure is particularly relevant as global fertilizer demand remains closely linked to agricultural procurement cycles. At the same time, sulphuric acid is used across metal processing, chemicals and other industrial applications, meaning tighter export availability can affect multiple downstream sectors.
	What Is the Outlook for Sulphuric Acid?
Russia's export restriction is likely to keep international sulphuric acid markets focused on alternative supply sources through the fourth quarter. The impact will depend on domestic Russian demand, the availability of acid from China and other exporters, sulphur availability, and global fertilizer consumption. With the Russian measure running until the end of December, any additional production or logistics disruptions elsewhere could amplify supply tightness and keep international buyers competing for replacement volumes.

Highlights
- Southern Copper is moving with firm base-metals prices as copper demand draws support from grids and data centers.
- Some of the largest copper reserves in the world and strong silver byproduct output set the producer apart.
- Project delivery in Peru and Mexico, cost control and community relations remain the themes the market tracks.
Southern Copper (NYSE:SCCO) Basic Materials Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO) 198.66 USD -1.910 0.952% Last Updated at: 2026-10-08T20:09:00Z is moving with firm base-metals prices as electrification, the data-center buildout and strong precious-metals trading keep industrial demand in focus, and the Arizona-headquartered producer is drawing steady attention as a result. Its mines sit in Peru and Mexico, and its reserves are among the deepest anywhere in the sector.
The backdrop is a market in the middle of a rotation. Artificial intelligence and semiconductor names set record levels early in the week, then eased as bond yields climbed and oil pushed back toward the hundred-dollar mark. Commodity-linked equities have drawn some of the money that stepped away from richly priced growth stocks.
For Southern Copper, the appeal is straightforward. The company produces copper at enormous scale, adds silver, molybdenum and zinc to the mix, and operates in a market where new supply is difficult to bring online. Each of those traits matters when prices are firm, and together they help explain why the stock often trades in sympathy with the metal.
Reserve life is the quality most often highlighted when the company is discussed. Its ore bodies in Peru and Mexico are large, and the company has pointed for years to a very long runway of production that stretches across multiple decades at current rates. Few competitors can claim anything similar.
That depth matters because the global copper industry faces a quiet problem. Many established mines are aging, ore grades are drifting lower and discoveries of large new deposits have become rare. A producer with long-lived reserves already in hand faces fewer questions about where the next ton of metal will come from.
The company is also majority controlled by a Mexican mining and transportation group, which provides a stable anchor and links the business to a railway and infrastructure network that helps move concentrate and supplies. That relationship shapes the culture of the business, which is generally described as conservative and focused on low-cost operations.
Copper in an Electrified World
Copper is the backbone of electrification. It carries current through cables, windings and busbars, and it is difficult to replace without sacrificing efficiency or raising costs. As power systems expand to serve electric vehicles, renewable generation and new industrial loads, the volume of copper embedded in the economy keeps rising.
Data centers amplify the trend. A modern computing campus uses large amounts of copper in power distribution, cooling systems and internal connections, and developers have been rushing to build capacity. Utilities in turn are planning grid upgrades, transmission lines and substations to serve those campuses.
The Silver and Molybdenum Kicker
One feature that sets Southern Copper apart from many peers is its role in silver. The company is among the largest producers of the white metal in the world, mainly as a byproduct of its copper and zinc operations. With precious metals trading firmly, that stream contributes a noticeable lift to earnings.
Silver has an unusual dual personality. It is a store of value that tends to follow gold, yet it is also an industrial input used in solar panels, electronics and electrical contacts. Demand from clean energy manufacturing adds a link to the same electrification theme that supports copper.
Operations in Peru
Peru is home to a large share of the company's output, with long-running open-pit operations, concentrators, a smelter and a refinery forming an integrated chain. Being able to process its own concentrate gives the business more control over costs and quality than a miner that ships raw material to third parties.
The country has also been the setting for one of the company's best-known growth stories, a coastal project that has faced years of community debate before moving forward. Progress there is closely followed, because it would add meaningful new volume and demonstrate that large projects can advance in a sensitive social setting.
Operations in Mexico
In Mexico, the company runs several large operations, including open-pit sites and underground units that produce copper, zinc, silver and molybdenum. The country is home to the parent group, which gives the business a long history and strong ties to local communities and suppliers.
Expansion work in Mexico is a recurring theme. New concentrator capacity and the development of additional deposits are intended to lift volumes over time, and the pace of construction is watched closely. These projects are large and complex, and timing can slip because of weather, supply chains or permitting.
Where It Fits Among Peers
Southern Copper is one of the larger names in the wider universe of metals and mining stocks. Comparisons with other copper producers usually focus on three themes: reserve life, unit costs and country exposure. On reserves and costs the company ranks near the top, while country concentration is the feature that draws the most debate.
Freeport-McMoRan, with its large operations in the United States, Peru and Indonesia, is the most frequent comparison, while global diversified miners bring wider commodity baskets. Southern Copper offers a more focused exposure to copper and silver without iron ore or coal to dilute the picture.
The Dividend Tradition
Distributions have long been part of the story. The company has paid sizable dividends in strong years, and the stance of sharing a large portion of earnings with owners is a hallmark that sets it apart from many growth-focused miners that retain cash for expansion.
Because payouts follow earnings, they swing with copper and silver. Firm prices tend to raise capacity, while weak prices narrow it. Market participants who prize steady distributions therefore treat metals strength as a supportive sign, even though the payout is never guaranteed.
What the Market Watches Next
With bank earnings opening and corporate reporting season approaching, attention will turn to updates on realized prices, production at the main sites, byproduct volumes and capital spending. Commentary on the pace of expansion work in both countries will receive particular scrutiny.
Broader macro signals will matter too. Data on Chinese industrial activity, American manufacturing and construction, and global electricity demand will shape sentiment toward base metals. Moves in the dollar and in bond yields will add another layer of influence on how the sector trades day to day.

The project is designed to produce approximately 2,000 tonnes per annum (tpa) of battery-grade lithium carbonate, with commissioning and initial production targeted for late 2027.

	For Aramco, the project represents an opportunity to leverage its decades of experience in subsurface resources and field operations beyond traditional hydrocarbons. For NESR, the agreement strengthens its position in the emerging lithium value chain and provides an opportunity to commercialize its DLE technology in one of the world's major energy-producing regions.
	The project is also supported by NESR’s existing regional experience across Saudi Arabia, including subsurface and field operations. This local expertise could help accelerate project execution and technology deployment.

Successful operation could provide a foundation for larger-scale lithium projects in Saudi Arabia and potentially support the development of a domestic battery-materials supply chain.

The immediate impact will be on battery-grade lithium carbonate supply, as the planned 2,000 tpa facility adds a new regional production source and demonstrates DLE technology at commercial scale. PRINCETON, NJ, Oct. 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Digital Asset Acquisition Corp. (Nasdaq: DAAQ) ("DAAQ”), a special purpose acquisition company, today announced that it has entered into a merger agreement (the "Merger Agreement” and the transactions contemplated by that agreement, the "Business Combination”) with Titan Strategics Holdings Ltd, a Cayman Islands exempted company ("Titan”), and the direct owner of one hundred percent (100%) of the equity interests in Titan Strategics AS, the exploration license holder over the former Ranstad uranium mine and the surrounding Billingen uranium district in Sweden. Upon closing, the combined company (the "Pubco”) is expected to operate under the new name of Renaissance Nuclear, Inc. The proposed Business Combination remains subject to the receipt of all necessary shareholder and regulatory approvals, and other customary closing conditions.
Titan Strategics AS holds the exploration permits for the Billingen Uranium Project in south-central Sweden, a district-scale land package that takes in the former Ranstad mine. Ranstad was the cornerstone of Sweden’s plan for nuclear fuel self-sufficiency and produced uranium from 1965 to 1969, until low prices at the time forced its closure. In the 1970s, LKAB became a co-manager and drew up plans to restart and expand it. Now, with the ban lifted, AI driving power demand and Europe racing to replace Russian nuclear fuel, Titan intends to bring this historic district back to life with modern exploration. The project sits about 5 kilometers from Skövde and 150 kilometers from Gothenburg, Scandinavia’s largest container port, with highway, rail and grid power already in place.
The proposed Business Combination will bring together proven leadership in mine development, nuclear energy and capital markets.
The combined company is expected to be led by Executive Chairman Adam Clode, a mining executive with more than 25 years’ experience taking projects from resource definition to production. Mr. Clode started his career developing a gold asset for Newmont Mining Corporation in Ghana; served as Site Manager at Equinox Minerals’ Lumwana copper project in Zambia (Equinox was later acquired by Barrick for approximately $7.8 billion); and, as Manager of Projects, delivered African Minerals’ $3 billion Tonkolili iron ore development in Sierra Leone through to first ore shipment, supporting the team that secured more than $2 billion in strategic funding. DAAQ Co-Chairmen Pete Ort and Jeff Tuder bring over 30 years of investing, advising and experience with special purpose acquisition companies, or SPACs. Their most recent SPAC, Real Asset Acquisition Corp. (Nasdaq: RAAQ), closed its combination with IQM Quantum Computers Oyj (Nasdaq: IQMX) in July 2026, creating the first European quantum computing company listed on a major U.S. exchange. DAAQ’s advisors add decades of uranium and nuclear operating experience.
Adam Clode, Executive Chairman of the post-closing combined business, commented: "Ranstad is where the Swedish state mined uranium to secure its energy independence. Today, the EU imports virtually every pound of the uranium its reactors need. We hold the licenses over Sweden’s largest formerly producing uranium mine and the district around it, backed by decades of state-funded drilling. Our plan is simple: recover the historical data, confirm it with modern drilling and build toward a maiden resource. DAAQ gives us the capital markets access to move fast.”
Peter Ort, Co-Chairman & Principal Executive Officer of DAAQ, added: "Titan has something genuinely rare: exploration rights over a formerly producing uranium mine inside the EU and NATO, in a country that has just reopened its doors to uranium. With the EU importing almost all of its uranium, we believe assets like Ranstad have strategic value the market has yet to recognize. We believe Titan is well-positioned to deliver meaningful value for shareholders.”
Europe’s Uranium Security Gap
EU reactors run almost entirely on imported uranium. In 2025, EU utilities received about 14,700 tonnes of natural uranium, all from outside the EU, around 16% of it from Russia (Euratom Supply Agency). Brussels’ REPowerEU roadmap aims to phase out remaining Russian energy imports, including nuclear. Demand is rising too: nuclear already supplies about 30% of Sweden’s electricity, the government plans the equivalent of up to ten new large reactors by 2045, and Vattenfall’s Videberg Kraft project has selected Rolls-Royce SMRs for Ringhals. Worldwide, AI and data centers are driving demand for always-on, carbon-free power, while industry analysts point to a structural gap between mine supply and reactor needs.
Billingen: A District-Scale Opportunity
Two exploration licenses, Billingen nr 100 and Billingen nr 200, cover approximately 207 km² (20,713 hectares). They were granted by the Swedish Mining Inspectorate on January 16, 2025, run to January 16, 2028 and can be extended under the Swedish Minerals Act, subject to approval by the Swedish Mining Inspectorate. They take in the Ranstad mine site and the Billingen plateau, where the uranium sits in a flat layer of alum shale that can be traced for kilometers.
According to Titan’s compilation and interpretation of historical Swedish government drilling records, between 1957 and 1975, the Swedish state drilled 242 holes across the Billingen area, more than 200 of them inside Titan’s license area. Assay records for the 11 holes drilled inside the license area in 1974-75 average approximately 350 ppm U3O8 (about 0.035%) over about 7 meters, with the best hole grading 564 ppm U3O8. On the eastern flank, drilling hit the uranium layer as shallow as about 9 meters. These historical results have not yet been verified by a Qualified Person under the Securities and Exchange Commission’s (the "SEC”) rules under Regulation S-K 1300 ("SK-1300”).
The same layer carries vanadium, molybdenum, nickel and zinc, and modern processing tested on comparable Swedish alum shale has shown the potential to recover vanadium alongside uranium. An independent "Qualified Person” (as defined in SK-1300) is preparing an SK-1300 Technical Report Summary.

The combined company expects to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, exploration and advancement of the Billingen Uranium Project, and transaction expenses.

Highlights
- PFS met testwork results near complete and showing consistency with historical results thus supporting PFS metallurgical assumptions and by-product recovery potential.
- Major flowsheet improvements achieved through 1) elimination of heap leach component, with all production via milling & flotation; 2) significant low grade material rejection through coarse particle flotation ("CPF") and 3) application of Jameson cells.
- Debottlenecking study has improved the PFS base case crushing throughput to 48 Mtpa, with CPF rejecting approximately 12 Mtpa of coarse gangue at 0.05% Cu ahead of flotation, resulting in 36 Mtpa of main flotation circuit throughput at higher copper grades.
- CPF is an advanced mineral processing method that enables efficient recovery of coarse mineral particles (up to 450µm in the Haib tests), thereby significantly increasing copper feed grade to the main flotation circuit.
- Extensive Jameson cell and CPF testwork completed with excellent results.
- Jameson cells in conjunction with conventional flotation will enable target copper recovery to be maintained while facilitating increased final concentrate copper grade and reduced power and space requirements for flotation.
- MoA signed with NamPower. Grid connection engineering underway with final system design expected in November. Power to be supplied via 68km 220kV grid connection from Harib substation, supplemented by solar PV and battery energy storage.
- MoU signed with NamWater. Infrastructure Development Agreement for bulk water supply system being developed. Orange River supply scheme selected as preferred, lowest-cost bulk water supply solution, with single abstraction point approximately 9 km south of the mine.
- Optimised tailings storage facility site selected from nine candidate locations, which will accommodate full ~1.15Bt of LOM tailings in single facility.
- ESIA and EMP supporting the Environmental Clearance Certificate application for the Mining License Area and Water Abstraction submitted to MEFT on 19 August 2026 and 04 September 2026 respectively, with a decision expected before the end of 2027.
- All workstreams on schedule to support PFS publication before the end of November 2026.
Luxembourg, Luxembourg--(Newsfile Corp. - October 8, 2026) - Koryx Copper S.A. (TSXV: KRY) (NSX: KYX) (OTCQX: KRYXF) ("Koryx" or the "Company") is pleased to provide an interim update on the progress of the technical and engineering studies being undertaken in support of the Pre-Feasibility Study ("PFS") for the wholly-owned Haib Copper Project ("Haib" or the "Project") in southern Namibia. The results of the PFS are expected to be press released before the end of November 2026.
Haib is a massive, disseminated porphyry Cu deposit with associated Mo and Au and is envisaged to produce a Cu and Mo concentrate via large-scale open pit mining and conventional sulphide milling and flotation.
Heye Daun, Koryx Copper's President & CEO commented: "With conversion drilling now completed for the PFS and our metallurgical, infrastructure and permitting workstreams all advancing in parallel, we remain firmly on track to deliver the Haib PFS before the end of November 2026. I am very pleased with the performance of our in-house study team, working in conjunction with our lead engineering consultants, DRA Global Limited, and a range of experienced Namibian technical consultants who are all working very hard to deliver a PFS, based on credible assumptions and detailed specialist technical studies. We are confident that this will be reflected in outstanding production and economic metrics which will benchmark the Haib Copper project as a rapidly advancing, world class copper development project in the south of Namibia".
Metallurgical Test Work
The core PFS metallurgical test work program is nearing completion, with most results currently in final review by the Project study team. Interim test work results show excellent continuity from prior test work completed on the Project. The PFS test work has also started to strengthen the Project team's understanding of by-product recovery potential in Haib's copper concentrates.
Jameson Cell and coarse particle flotation (''CPF'') for pre-concentration continues to strongly support the proposed base case processing flowsheet as the preferred approach to maximizing early gangue rejection, final concentrate grades and overall metal recovery.
Coarse particle flotation introduces water and/or air to maintain a fluidised bed in specialised low turbulence flotation cells. In the Haib tests, partially liberated sulphides up to 450 µm in diameter were successfully floated. This will enable coarse gangue to be rejected and discarded instead of the conventional approach of milling all run of mine material (including gangue) finely ahead of conventional flotation, which requires much more milling energy per unit of mineralised material.
Testing of selected samples of transitional mineralized material with copper mineralization occurring as mainly primary and secondary copper sulfides is expected to be completed in early October and give the study team guidance on its flotation response and opportunity for processing via conventional flotation.
The metallurgical program for the definitive feasibility study (DFS) is well underway with drill core and pilot bulk metallurgical sample selection having commenced in August. The sample selection is focused on the building of a comprehensive geo-metallurgical model for both comminution and flotation aspects of the Project during the DFS planned for 2027.
Process Plant Design
Process plant design work is progressing well with the process flow diagrams and process design criteria currently in review and near finalized. A debottlenecking study of the process plant done by Koryx lead PFS engineering consultants, DRA Global Limited, has fixed the PFS base case capacity to process a total of 48 million tons per year (Mtpa) of run of mine ("ROM") material via three stages of crushing (gyratory, secondary cone with screen sizing, and tertiary high pressure grinding rolls), ball milling with CPF being applied to the -425 +150 µm size range of the recirculating load and rejecting approximately 12 Mtpa of coarse gangue at 0.05% Cu before the flotation circuit. The remainder of the circuit will be a hybrid of conventional tank cells and Jameson cells due to their enhanced overall flotation performance. The secondary flotation circuit will continue to produce both a bulk clean primary copper concentrate and a smaller molybdenum rich copper concentrate.
Heap leaching of approximately 50 million tons of oxide copper mineralized material is no longer expected to form part of the PFS base case, but provision for it will remain in the overall layout. The comprehensive metallurgical and process engineering work on heap leaching is being concluded to a prefeasibility level and heap leaching is expected to remain an option for the Project in the future.
The plant layout has been finalised to optimise the use of the Project terrain and minimise conveying distances, bulk earthworks, mine-to-crusher haul distances, utility requirements, and the overall footprint of processing and mining services. It also allows for future expansion through additional front-end and flotation circuits, should the Project be expanded.
Tailings Storage Facility
During the PFS process, the tailings storage facility ("TSF") site selection has undergone extensive development and rationalisation, particularly as the envisaged tonnage has increased because of resource and processing optimisations, and updated layout of the proposed mine site. The team identified and assessed nine potential sites at various locations within and surrounding the exploration lease area.
Nine potential sites were evaluated using a multi-criteria matrix assessment. The criteria considered costs, capacity, dam breach risks, environmental, social and design issues as well as storage efficiencies for the starter and final embankments. This process resulted in the selection of an optimised site that could most cost-efficiently contain 1.15 Bt and is the only location able to accept the full LOM quantity of tailings in one facility, as well as having a relatively low environmental impact. This position is also the most proximal to the revised plant location and has the added benefit to optimise operating costs of the TSF through short pumping distances.
Mine Bulk Power Supply
With the expected increase in the process plant throughput to 48 Mtpa, the Project's electricity requirements have increased accordingly. The current power demand estimate is 260 MVA maximum demand and annual electricity consumption is estimated as 1.45 TWh, reflecting the larger scale of the operation and associated infrastructure requirements.
The Project's power supply strategy remains centered on a connection to the NamPower grid, supplemented by solar photovoltaic (PV) generation and the integration of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to reduce overall energy costs and manage peak tariff periods. The planned double-circuit 68km long 220 kV overhead transmission line from Harib substation to the mine site remains the preferred and technically robust solution, and is expected to provide sufficient scalability to support the Project's long-term development plans.
Koryx continues to work closely with NamPower under the existing Memorandum of Understanding. NamPower is currently reassessing the implications of the increased load forecast on the transmission network and will provide an updated power supply offer, which is expected to form the basis of the final power supply agreement.
The Project is expected to deliver significant new transmission infrastructure and network upgrades in southern Namibia, which are intended to strengthen the regional grid and will ultimately be transferred to NamPower for operation and maintenance.

Key Highlights
- Hercules Metals closed down 5.00% on October 07, 2026, reflecting renewed selling pressure and weaker near-term sentiment.
- The company is advancing a major copper exploration story in Idaho, but its valuation remains closely tied to exploration success and future development expectations.
- Recent exploration progress provides long-term potential, although investors remain exposed to drilling outcomes, funding requirements, Commodity cycles, and project execution.
- Copper-market Volatility and broader risk-off conditions can amplify price swings across junior Mining equities.
- The recent decline highlights the gap between long-term discovery potential and near-term investor expectations.
- A sustained recovery will likely depend on continued exploration success, stronger confidence in the project's scale, and improved visibility around development.
Introduction
Hercules Metals Corp. (TSXV:BIG) is a U.S.-focused mineral exploration company advancing its Hercules Project in western Idaho, where it is exploring a large copper system alongside silver-lead-zinc mineralization. The flagship project hosts the Leviathan porphyry copper discovery, while continued exploration is targeting additional mineralized centres across the broader land position.
Despite the project's considerable exploration potential, Hercules Metals stock came under pressure on October 07, 2026, declining 5.00% as market sentiment toward the shares weakened. As an exploration-stage mining company, the stock remains highly sensitive to drilling results, commodity expectations, financing conditions, liquidity, and speculative positioning. This creates a potentially wide gap between long-term geological potential and short-term market performance.
The broader mining environment also remains challenging for higher-risk exploration equities. While copper continues to benefit from long-term electrification, infrastructure, and supply-demand themes, junior miners can experience substantial volatility when investors become more selective or shift Capital toward established producers. Consequently, even positive project developments may not immediately translate into sustained share-price momentum.
Key Reasons Behind Decline
Weak investor sentiment: The recent red close indicates that near-term market conviction has weakened. Exploration companies often experience sharp sentiment-driven movements because valuation depends heavily on expectations surrounding future discoveries rather than established operating cash flows.
Sector weakness: Junior mining equities remain vulnerable to changes in risk appetite across the broader commodities market. When investors rotate toward lower-risk Assets or established producers, exploration companies can experience disproportionate selling pressure.
Operational challenges: Hercules continues to depend on systematic exploration and drilling to establish the scale and quality of its mineral systems. The company's Leviathan discovery has demonstrated significant exploration potential, but additional drilling remains important for improving geological confidence and defining future development prospects.
Exploration execution: The Investment case depends heavily on successful drilling, geological interpretation, target generation, and resource definition. Any disappointing results or delays in converting exploration success into a more clearly defined development opportunity could pressure investor expectations.
Commodity volatility: Copper prices remain a major external influence. Strong long-term copper fundamentals can support exploration valuations, but short-term commodity volatility can quickly affect sentiment toward development-stage and exploration-stage companies.
Funding pressure: Exploration businesses generally require continued access to capital to maintain drilling and development programs. Hercules recently completed a private Placement led by its incoming Leadership team, demonstrating the importance of financing capacity to its exploration strategy. Future capital requirements could create additional dilution concerns if exploration spending remains elevated.
Speculative selling: Hercules Metals has attracted substantial interest because of the potential scale of its copper discovery. Such interest can also increase trading volatility, particularly when momentum reverses and speculative investors reduce exposure.
Declining Earnings visibility: Unlike established producers, Hercules does not have a mature production base generating predictable operating earnings. Consequently, investors must primarily assess geological potential, exploration progress, capital requirements, and the probability of eventual project development.
Institutional positioning: Changes in institutional and sophisticated-investor risk appetite can have an outsized impact on junior mining stocks. A reduction in exposure to speculative resources can create additional downside even without a major deterioration in the underlying project.
Geopolitical and macroeconomic pressure: The US-Iran conflict and broader geopolitical tensions can increase uncertainty across global commodity markets. Energy-price volatility can contribute to inflationary pressure, while concerns about global growth can weaken Demand expectations for industrial commodities. Although Hercules operates in the United States and therefore has relatively limited direct exposure to Middle Eastern operations, the company remains indirectly exposed through commodity prices, investor risk appetite, inflation, financing conditions, and global economic uncertainty.
Risks to Consider
Regulatory uncertainty: Mining development requires compliance with environmental, land-use, permitting, and other regulatory requirements. While Hercules benefits from its Idaho location and existing land position, future development would still involve regulatory and technical considerations.
Competition: Copper exploration is attracting significant capital as investors anticipate future Supply constraints. Hercules must compete for capital, technical expertise, investor attention, and strategic interest against numerous exploration and development companies.
Funding risk: Continued exploration requires capital. Additional financing could increase the company's share count and create dilution for existing shareholders, particularly if market conditions deteriorate.
Operational execution risk: Exploration programs involve geological uncertainty. Drilling results can vary materially between targets, and successful discoveries do not automatically translate into economically viable mines.
Commodity price weakness: A sustained decline in copper or other relevant metals could reduce the attractiveness of exploration assets and weaken the valuation investors are willing to assign to Hercules.
Geopolitical exposure: Global geopolitical instability can affect commodity prices, inflation, interest rates, currencies, and investor risk tolerance. These indirect effects can be particularly significant for speculative mining equities.
Project delays: Delays in drilling, interpretation, permitting, technical studies, or future development could push expected milestones further into the future and reduce near-term investor enthusiasm.
Weak market conditions: A broader correction in equities or commodities could create additional selling pressure regardless of company-specific exploration progress.
Liquidity concerns: Junior mining stocks can experience larger price movements when Liquidity weakens. This can amplify both upward and downward moves and make investor sentiment more influential.
Recessionary pressure: A deterioration in global economic activity could weaken industrial commodity expectations and reduce risk capital available for exploration companies.
Energy and industrial volatility: Higher energy and input costs can increase the eventual cost of exploration and mine development, while weaker industrial demand could pressure copper-related valuations.
Valuation Perspective
Hercules Metals presents a valuation challenge because its Market Value is largely linked to the perceived future potential of its exploration assets rather than established production earnings. This makes traditional earnings-based valuation metrics less useful and places greater emphasis on geological potential, resource growth, exploration success, management execution, and the possibility of eventual project development.
The Leviathan copper system provides an important foundation for the investment case, with the company continuing to explore its scale and identify additional porphyry centres. Recent work has also expanded exploration activity toward targets such as Southern Flats, Pegasus, and Hook.
However, the market may already incorporate a meaningful portion of the company's exploration potential. This creates a risk of a valuation reset if future drilling fails to meet elevated expectations. The recent share-price weakness therefore highlights the possibility that investors are becoming more demanding about evidence of continued discovery growth.
There is also a potential mismatch between geological potential and development certainty. A large discovery can create significant long-term value, but establishing a commercially viable mining operation requires additional exploration, resource definition, engineering work, capital investment, permitting, infrastructure, and favorable commodity conditions.

Shell Canada Energy announced it has reached final investment decision (FID) on its LNG Canada Phase 2 in Kitimat, British Columbia. Shell reports Phase 2 will double total production capacity at the Kitimat facility from 14 mtpa to 28 mtpa. Two LNG trains will be added to the facility, along with a new LNG storage tank, condensate tank, loading berth, and expanded utility and process systems. Coastal GasLink will expand the capacity of the existing 670-km pipeline through the construction of five new compressor stations.
The Kitimat facility is the first large-scale LNG export facility in Canada, with an annual production capacity of up to 14 mtpa in Phase 1.
Global engineering firm JGC Corporation and Texas-based engineering and construction firm Fluor Corporation received notice to proceed for Phase 2. The companies previously provided front-end engineering and design and engineering, procurement, and construction services for Phase 1.
Shell said the facility will supply cost-competitive gas to Asian markets, where demand for LNG is expected to increase significantly.
"LNG Canada is a core part of our Integrated Gas portfolio, helping to supply LNG to customers in Asia at a time when diversity of energy supplies and energy security are increasingly important,” said Cederic Cremers, Shell’s Integrated Gas president.
Shell will receive approximately 6 mtpa of additional LNG from the expansion with commercial operations expected to begin in the early 2030s.
LNG Canada is a joint venture in which Shell holds a 40% interest, with partners Petronas (25%), PetroChina Company Ltd. (15%), Mitsubishi Corporation (15%), and Korea Gas Corporation (5%).

The Port of Galveston has approved a lease and development agreement with Power LNG for a small-scale LNG production, storage and bunkering facility on Pelican Island.
The 30-acre greenfield site sits on the east side of an 82-acre port-owned tract on Galveston Harbour.
Power LNG plans to build two modular liquefaction trains, each producing about 200,000 gallons per day, for an initial capacity of 400,000 gallons daily. The company said it could later expand the plant to 800,000 gallons per day.
The project includes an underground natural gas pipeline, a 3m-gallon LNG storage tank and a shore-to-ship pier for fueling vessels and bunker barges. LNG bunkering operations are expected to serve ships in the Galveston, Houston, and Texas City channels.
Commercial production is targeted for the fourth quarter of 2028, subject to permits, financing and other agreements.
“This agreement paves the way for the Port of Galveston to play a leading role in providing cleaner marine fuels to the region,” said Rodger Rees, port director and chief executive. “As more LNG-powered ships are built, demand for LNG marine fuel is reaching a tipping point.”
Power LNG chief executive Austin Terry said the company would develop an integrated solution covering liquefaction, storage, bunkering, vessel loading and export.
The port and Power LNG also plan to negotiate future agreements for LNG and ISO tank container loading at an adjacent dock, with possible additional activities at Piers 34 and 39.
The facility, known internally as Project Seawolf, is estimated to cost about $240m in its initial phase.

articles.title: Advanced Sorbent Technology Selectively Extracts Lithium Chloride From Complex Brines - AZoCleantech

With support from U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) National Laboratories, including Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), Texas-based company Element3 has launched the first domestic lithium mining project in 50 years. This achievement is likely to have a big impact, turning the United States from a net importer of lithium to a country well on the path to greater energy independence, national security, and economic strength.
The milestone, in February 2026, came less than a year after DOE launched the Minerals to Materials Supply Chain Research Facility, or METALLIC, in April 2025. The facility builds on DOE demonstration testbeds to speed technologies that strengthen the nation's supply chain of minerals critical to the technology, transportation, and defense industries. It provides experts and tools to de-risk development of these critical minerals technologies.
National Labs Help Partners Strengthen Their Domestic Supply Chains
Led by the National Energy Technology Laboratory, nine DOE National Labs operate four METALLIC centers. The centers focus on improving feedstock purity, extracting and separating minerals using energy-saving methods, refining salts and oxides into metals, and developing alloys for advanced manufacturing.
Companies and universities work with the national labs to test and validate technologies as they progress from the lab scale to pilot plants. The centers connect technology developers, suppliers, and users to strengthen U.S. supply chains for critical minerals including rare earth elements, platinum group metals, lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, gallium, and germanium.
"We want to optimize material processing methods, reduce environmental impact and recover more value from materials," said ORNL's Parans Paranthaman, who leads METALLIC's Extractions and Separations Center.
The center is co-led by Argonne and Idaho national laboratories. Partners include Ames, Lawrence Berkeley, Lawrence Livermore and Pacific Northwest national laboratories and the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The team works to expand and diversify mineral sources and test new extraction methods, including chemistry guided by Super Intelligence (SI).
ORNL's METALLIC team provides diverse expertise. Chemists and chemical engineers including Ramesh Bhave, Barbara Evans, Syed Islam, Jayanthi Kumar, Katie Johnson, Bruce Moyer, Pasindu Samaraweera, Saurabh Prakash Pethe, Shailesh Dangwal and Donga Kang provide expertise in membranes, solvent extraction and absorption methods to find new ways to extract lithium, gallium, germanium, and rare earths. Physical chemist Craig Bridges designs SI-enabled autonomous labs for process optimization. Nanomaterials experts Rigoberto Advincula and Ilia Ivanov use ORNL's Center for Nanophase Materials Sciences to probe characteristics of columns packed with sorbents that separate lithium from brine. Other ORNL staff members, interns, graduate students, and postdoctoral researchers contribute as well.
"We want industry partners to come and use the national lab capabilities and test their systems," Paranthaman said.
New Lithium Supply Strengthens U.S. Security, Economy
Element3 focuses on extracting lithium from wastewater generated during oil production in the Permian Basin. Back in 2024, the company had licensed technology that was batteries" developed by Paranthaman's ORNL team. The innovation won an R&D 100 Award that year. Recently, this team won the 2026 Excellence in Technology Transfer Award from the Federal Laboratory Consortium.
The process selectively extracts lithium from produced water, which is derived from oil and gas extraction. This wastewater contains lithium. Leveraging ORNL's technology, the company recovers lithium chloride and converts it to battery-grade lithium carbonate powder.
"The feedstock contains all kinds of elements, so you need to selectively extract the element of interest with high efficiency and low cost as you scale up," Paranthaman said.
On Feb. 6, Paranthaman attended a ribbon-cutting to celebrate the opening of Element3's lithium extraction plant in Midland, Texas. The plant extracts lithium chloride from produced water and converts it to lithium carbonate.
Element3 has now deployed its first commercial lithium extraction plant in the Permian Basin using ORNL technology. This completes the scaling of the technology from the laboratory to a commercial operation. It marks the first new lithium mining project to market in the United States since the late 1960s.
Element3's lithium carbonate facility can produce 3,000 tons of lithium per year - nearly half of the current U.S. production. Lithium is used in some vehicle batteries and smartphones and could help provide grid-scale energy storage.
For decades, much lithium processing has occurred overseas, where labor is cheaper and environmental protections are less stringent. This facility signals a shift toward U.S.-based production.
"We can produce our own starting materials, like for battery manufacturing for example," Paranthaman said. "You need lithium hydroxide or lithium carbonate, and we are producing those chemicals at the Texas site. We are doing the separation to produce our own lithium. This is a domestic supply chain."
"Thanks to the support of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, we have been able to leverage existing technology to solve our challenges and accelerate our path to market," said Element3 chief executive officer Hood Whitson.
"The success of Element3 is what METALLIC's innovation ecosystem aims to emulate with keystone companies," Paranthaman said.
The Critical Materials Innovation Hub and Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office, which are part of an Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation effort, supported the initial development of ORNL work.
UT-Battelle manages ORNL for DOE's Office of Science, the single largest supporter of basic research in the physical sciences in the United States. The Office of Science is working to address some of the most pressing challenges of our time.
